sections.heading: The legal rule
sections.body:
324. (1) Whoever with intent to cause, or knowing that he is likely to cause, wrongful loss or damage to the public or to any person, causes the destruction of any property, or any such change in any property or in the situation thereof as destroys or diminishes its value or utility, or affects it injuriously, commits mischief
(2) Whoever commits mischief shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to six months, or with fine, or with both
(3) Whoever commits mischief and thereby causes loss or damage to any property including the property of Government or Local Authority shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to one year, or with fine, or with both
(4) Whoever commits mischief and thereby causes loss or damage to the amount of twenty thousand rupees and more but less than one lakh rupees shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to two years, or with fine, or with both
(5) Whoever commits mischief and thereby causes loss or damage to the amount of one lakh rupees or upwards, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to five years, or with fine, or with both
(6) Whoever commits mischief, having made preparation for causing to any person death, or hurt, or wrongful restraint, or fear of death, or of hurt, or of wrongful restraint, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to five years, and shall also be liable to fine

(6) Whoever commits mischief, having made preparation for causing to any person death, or hurt, or wrongful restraint, or fear of death, or of hurt, or of wrongful restraint, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to five years, and shall also be liable to fine

sections.heading: Statutory illustrations
sections.body:
(a) A voluntarily burns a valuable security belonging to Z intending to cause wrongful loss to Z. A has committed mischief
(b) A introduces water into an ice-house belonging to Z and thus causes the ice to melt, intending wrongful loss to Z. A has committed mischief
(c) A voluntarily throws into a river a ring belonging to Z, with the intention of thereby causing wrongful loss to Z. A has committed mischief
(d) A, knowing that his effects are about to be taken in execution in order to satisfy a debt due from him to Z, destroys those effects, with the intention of thereby preventing Z from obtaining satisfaction of the debt, and of thus causing damage to Z. A has committed mischief
(e) A having insured a ship, voluntarily causes the same to be cast away, with the intention of causing damage to the underwriters. A has committed mischief
(f) A causes a ship to be cast away, intending thereby to cause damage to Z who has lent money on bottomry on the ship. A has committed mischief
(g) A, having joint property with Z in a horse, shoots the horse, intending thereby to cause wrongful loss to Z. A has committed mischief
(h) A causes cattle to enter upon a field belonging to Z, intending to cause and knowing that he is likely to cause damage to Z’s crop. A has committed mischief

sections.heading: Explanations
sections.body:
Explanation 1.—It is not essential to the offence of mischief that the offender should intend to cause loss or damage to the owner of the property injured or destroyed. It is sufficient if he intends to cause, or knows that he is likely to cause, wrongful loss or damage to any person by injuring any property, whether it belongs to that person or not
Explanation 2.—Mischief may be committed by an act affecting property belonging to the person who commits the act, or to that person and others jointly

questionsAndAnswers.question: Legal Assessment & Statutory Note: BNS s. 324 (Mischief)
questionsAndAnswers.answer:
Introduction. BNS s. 324 deals with Mischief. It sits in Chapter XVII — Of Offences Against Property of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023. After 1 July 2024 this is the current-law citation for this offence / definition / punishment.

Meaning. Mischief (old 425/426): intending or knowing it likely to cause wrongful loss or damage, causing destruction or a situation that diminishes value or utility. BNS restatement of IPC 425 / 426. Cite the BNS number for facts on or after 1 July 2024.

Legal rule. In student language: BNS s. 324 is the rule on “Mischief”. The section provides that (1) Whoever with intent to cause, or knowing that he is likely to cause, wrongful loss or damage to the public or to any person, causes the destruction of any property, or any such change in any property or in the situation thereof as destroys or diminishes its value or utility, or affects it injuriously, commits mischief. Do not stop at the heading. An examiner awards marks for the ingredients, the explanations and the illustrations, not for writing the title alone.

Essential ingredients. An authoritative analysis must list them, not hide them in one paragraph:
1. (1) Whoever with intent to cause, or knowing that he is likely to cause, wrongful loss or damage to the public or to any person, causes the destruction of any property, or any such change in any property or in the situation thereof as destroys or diminishes its value or utility, or affects it injuriously, commits mischief
2. (2) Whoever commits mischief shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to six months, or with fine, or with both
3. (3) Whoever commits mischief and thereby causes loss or damage to any property including the property of Government or Local Authority shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to one year, or with fine, or with both
4. (4) Whoever commits mischief and thereby causes loss or damage to the amount of twenty thousand rupees and more but less than one lakh rupees shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to two years, or with fine, or with both
5. (5) Whoever commits mischief and thereby causes loss or damage to the amount of one lakh rupees or upwards, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to five years, or with fine, or with both
6. (6) Whoever commits mischief, having made preparation for causing to any person death, or hurt, or wrongful restraint, or fear of death, or of hurt, or of wrongful restraint, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to five years, and shall also be liable to fine

Illustrations. The section itself supplies worked examples. In legal analysis, pick one illustration, restate its facts, and show which ingredient it proves. Illustration (a): (a) A voluntarily burns a valuable security belonging to Z intending to cause wrongful loss to Z. A has committed mischief

Explanations. Explanation 1.—It is not essential to the offence of mischief that the offender should intend to cause loss or damage to the owner of the property injured or destroyed. It is sufficient if he intends to cause, or knows that he is likely to cause, wrongful loss or damage to any person by injuring any property, whether it belongs to that person or not An explanation is not optional commentary. It is part of the section and must appear in an authoritative brief.

Limitations. Apply only the conditions written in s. 324. Do not import a defence from a different chapter unless the question requires it.

Conclusion. BNS s. 324 is the complete current-law heading for Mischief. Define, list ingredients, use an illustration, note any explanation or exception, apply, cite. That is a complete statutory structure.

enhancement.detailedExplanation: Section 324 constitutes a key component of Chapter XVII (Of Offences against Property) of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, addressing mischief. The provision balances personal liberty with public interest and social order. The prosecution must establish every statutory element beyond reasonable doubt: the specified actus reus, the requisite mens rea, and any relevant statutory circumstances. Modern judicial interpretation emphasizes substantive fairness, proportionality in sentencing, and adherence to constitutional safeguards. Where statutory exceptions or provisos are attached to the section, the accused must establish facts bringing the case within such provisions under evidentiary standards.
examples: Teaching example (Standard application): An individual intentionally commits acts satisfying the statutory formula of mischief under Section 324 without lawful authority. The individual is liable under BNS s. 324.

Teaching example (Absence of mens rea / Lawful exception): A person acts in good faith or without the requisite statutory mental element under circumstances recognized by law. The essential ingredients of Section 324 are not satisfied; no penal liability attaches.
distinctions: Section 324 vs General Attempt: Section 324 penalizes the substantive conduct specified in Chapter XVII; inchoate attempts without specific provisions fall under the general attempt provisions.
Section 324 vs Cognate Chapter Offences: Liability under Section 324 is distinguished by its specific mental threshold and the particular legal interest protected under Of Offences against Property.
problemApplication: Issue: Whether the accused is liable under BNS s. 324 for conduct relating to mischief.
Rule: Under BNS s. 324, liability attaches upon proof of the statutory actus reus accompanied by the requisite mens rea without lawful justification.
Application: The evidence demonstrates that the accused performed the specified act with the required state of mind, satisfying all statutory ingredients of Section 324.
Conclusion: The accused is guilty of an offence under BNS s. 324 and subject to the prescribed punishment.
